newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian budget seen neutral-weaker for shares.
newsitem.headline: Australian budget seen neutral-weaker for shares.

text.p: The Australian budget is likely to have a neutral to slightly negative longer term impact on the record-breaking Australian share market, analysts said on Tuesday evening.

"There is some disappointment for the 1997/98 projected underlying deficit figures. We would have been looking for an underlying deficit of around A$1.5 billion," said Shane Oliver, chief economist at Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP).
The government projected an underlying shortfall of A$3.9 billion, around A$2.0 billion more than analysts had hoped for.
Oliver said the budget's longer term goals were more in line with what the market was looking for but the 1997/98 target would effectively delay the implied reduction in public debt.
Trading in the June Share Price Index (SPI) was unaffected by the budget but the Australian dollar slid half a U.S. cent in brisk trade and bond futures also dropped sharply in an immediate response.

Analysts said the most significant negative factor for the equity market was the government's planned crackdown on the trading of franking credits, known as dividend washing, and on dividend streaming to protect the tax base.

Dividend washing is a form of arbitrage between Australian and overseas shareholders used to exploit the value of dividend franking credits. The practice has led to large short term trades in blue chip Australian companies.

"It will have an immediate effect, it means that for offshore investors Australian shares will become a little less attractive than they were before," said Phillip Graham, senior economist at ANZ Securities.
"The other angle is those companies that have made use of dividend washing to boost their ability to frank their dividends will be made worse off as well," Graham said.

Analysts said the asset sale proceeds estimate of A$5.01 billion for 1998/99 suggested that the planned sale of the nation's telecommunications carrier, Telstra Corp, could be held via an instalment payment, similar to that used for the sale of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
Graham said an instalment arrangement for Testra was positive for the share market.
"There's nothing wrong with doing it that way. It is a very big float and it's probably good in that it spreads the load. It's a large issue for the market to swallow," he said.
The sale is tipped by analysts to raise about A$8 billion.
Simon Calder, chief economist at Melbourne broker J.B. Were and Son, said he did not expect the share market to have any significant reaction to the budget in the short term.
"I think the shares will open according to what happens (in offshore markets) overnight," Calder said.
The budget had no implications for monetary policy but it continued to leave open the possibility of a sovereign credit upgrading at some stage.
"By-and-large there are no surprises here.".
Calder said the government's key economic forecasts were reasonable-to-conservative.
"Certainly if you accept their (the government's) view that the unemployment rate will fall to 8.0 percent, that's another nail in the coffin of a further easing," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
